note: Action signals per rule, derived from each rule's own statement (not from the production trigger table). mode exact: the rule's trigger IS the action, so the label is the signal alone. signal_implies_gold: every case carrying the signal is gold for that rule whatever its score; cases without it are reviewed as usual. Other review entries only force the case into the review set. A squash merge counts as a commit boundary for every rule whose trigger is a commit or merge boundary.

signals.trigger: The moment a session is about to Write/Edit a .md file: route the content to the database unless the file is on the machine-required manifest.
signals.why: Write/Edit of a .md path is the stated binding moment; the manifest exception and the surface-registry clause need review. The condition needs a reader, so the signal only routes the case to adjudication; it does not force gold.

signals.trigger: A .md file created or modified through a shell redirect or tee.
signals.why: A shell write of a .md file is the same act the rule governs (the guard blocks .md create/modify). The condition needs a reader, so the signal only routes the case to adjudication; it does not force gold.

signals.trigger: At the moment a session spawns any subagent or workflow (or sizes a ~30+ minute item) it picks the cheapest executor and states an executor line.
signals.why: Spawning a subagent is the rule's own first trigger, so every Agent call binds; the 30-minute sizing clause can bind turns with no spawn.

signals.trigger: When a Salesforce diff CHANGED row proposes a phase move, never apply a backwards move from closed.
signals.why: A run of the Salesforce diff is necessary; whether it produced a backwards phase row needs review.

signals.trigger: Applying a Salesforce-proposed phase change through the deal update verbs.
signals.why: Writing a deal phase is where the hold applies; whether it came from the Salesforce diff and moves backwards needs review.

signals.trigger: A squash merge (gh pr merge that merges, including --auto) is a commit boundary.
signals.why: An act written into a commit message: a squash merge writes the commit message.

signals.trigger: When a session writes an act into a commit message (or close-out, decision entry, partner report), the diff must carry that act.
signals.why: Commit messages state acts; each case needs review against its diff.

signals.trigger: Same rule, for a decision entry or close-out written through a verb.
signals.why: Decision entries and loop close-outs are named writing moments; whether they claim an act needs review.

signals.trigger: Client and company documents default to Microsoft formats (docx/pptx/xlsx), not Google-native.
signals.why: Preparing a client/company document is the moment; the format chosen needs review.

signals.trigger: Before `git checkout -b` / `git checkout <branch>` in a shared checkout, claim the working tree or use a worktree.
signals.why: Branch creation or switching is the stated moment; whether the checkout is shared (not an isolated worktree) needs review.

signals.trigger: Cross-dataset identity match: a lone surname never merges; a second corroborating field is required, else flag 'possible match, confirm'.
signals.why: A merge call is where the threshold binds; matching done before any merge call can also bind.

signals.trigger: Reading meetings/attendees from local calendar stores or the published feed.
signals.why: Local calendar reads are the moment the rule governs (and the published feed is never a participant list).

signals.trigger: When reaching for the partner's meetings, attendees or mail: read the local Apple stores, never the Google connector.
signals.why: Connector calendar/mail reads are the act the rule forbids for the partner's data; whose data was sought needs review.

signals.trigger: The moment a session makes its FIRST write to tracked files in ~/carr-system: take an isolated worktree first.
signals.why: A file write is necessary; whether it is the first write to a tracked file in the canonical tree needs review.

signals.trigger: A squash merge (gh pr merge that merges, including --auto) is a commit boundary.
signals.why: Boundary sweep before a commit: a squash merge writes a commit to main.

signals.trigger: Boundary sweep for untaught rulings before any commit or deploy (also before a handoff/checkpoint and on subject change).
signals.why: Commit and deploy are named detectable sweep moments; the rule's seven partner-speech triggers are not actions. The production-migration script is a deploy. A commit, deploy and squash merge are treated alike: the signal routes the case to adjudication (a dry run is not a deploy), it does not force gold.

signals.trigger: Boundary sweep before writing a checkpoint.
signals.why: Writing a checkpoint is a named sweep moment.

signals.trigger: Same trigger as above, reached through the ./run.sh call door.
signals.why: Bash door to the same confirm-merge verb.

signals.trigger: Any merge of a duplicate-party pair runs (confirm-merge): survivorship precedence and the pre-merge orphan sweep bind.
signals.why: The rule binds 'before any merge runs' and decides which row survives once the pair is confirmed; confirm-merge is that merge.

signals.trigger: Outbound documents: LOIs and letters go in Word; spreadsheets go as PDF.
signals.why: Preparing or sending an outbound document is the moment; which document type and format needs review.

signals.trigger: When a migration adds or modifies a trigger or invoker-rights function: grant-check every table it reads, as the firing role.
signals.why: Writing trigger/function DDL in a migration is the stated moment.

signals.trigger: A CARR agent's own phone/email in a client, lead, vendor or party contact field is a placeholder: treat as null, never import, send to, or count it.
signals.why: Writing contact fields or sending to a contact is where a placeholder could be imported or used; whether one is present needs review.

signals.trigger: For any X (the site)/X retrieval, Grok Build is the first move; Chrome only for logged-in surfaces; never WebFetch.
signals.why: A retrieval call or delegated brief aimed at X is the trigger; which route was used needs review.

signals.trigger: When a session adds or edits a health row, alarm, meter or trend surface (touching tools/health-check.py or an ops/ check script).
signals.why: Editing those files is the rule's named detectable moment; whether a metric was added/edited needs review.

signals.trigger: Same trigger through the ./run.sh call door.
signals.why: Bash door to add-loop.

signals.trigger: Before opening any open_loop: name a real outside blocker from the closed list, or do the work and file nothing.
signals.why: add-loop is the filing act; only kind open_loop is gated (team_loop, action_required, idea are not), so each call needs review.

signals.trigger: When a session delegates any task to another seat, the dispatch names the specific model and effort level.
signals.why: An Agent spawn is a delegation, so every Agent call binds; delegation via a message to a running seat or an outside CLI can also bind.

signals.trigger: Delegation to an outside-model CLI seat (codex/grok/flash-run).
signals.why: Dispatching work to an outside CLI seat is a delegation, the rule's trigger.

signals.trigger: When a loop row is closed for a bookkeeping reason (renumber, merge, split): use dropped and say superseded, not abandoned, in the first words.
signals.why: close-loop is necessary; whether the close is bookkeeping needs review.

signals.trigger: Delegating the build or review of a scheduled job, launchd agent or automated chain.
signals.why: A brief that builds/fixes a scheduled job is the build moment, delegated.

signals.trigger: When any scheduled job, cron task, launchd agent or automated chain is built or reviewed: it must not depend on an interactive credential.
signals.why: Creating/updating a scheduled task is building one; whether it authenticates needs review.

signals.trigger: Building or reviewing a launchd agent or cron job.
signals.why: Touching launchd/cron plists or loads is the scheduled-job build/review moment.

signals.trigger: Any name/label write on a shared-by-design row: count attachments first; if more than one, mint a new row and re-point instead of renaming.
signals.why: A name/label field write is necessary; whether the row is shared-by-design needs review.

signals.trigger: Drafts for the partner's action are emailed from the AI Gmail to the partner's own work address; auto-send only to that one address.
signals.why: An email send/draft call is necessary; whether it is a handover draft and to whom needs review.

signals.trigger: Modelling a franchise/multi-location brand: one national account, each franchisee its own sub-client and its own deal.
signals.why: Creating a national account or its market deals is the modelling act; deal attachment through other verbs can also bind.

signals.trigger: A command a session issues or stores never names a private key path.
signals.why: A command or stored task naming key material is exactly the act the rule forbids.

signals.trigger: A session that changes code works in its own worktree and owns branch, checks, PR, merge, verification and cleanup.
signals.why: Editing a code file makes it a coding session; whether the shared checkout was used and delivery was owned needs review. The condition needs a reader, so the signal only routes the case to adjudication; it does not force gold.

signals.trigger: Same trigger through the ./run.sh call door.
signals.why: Bash door to teach/amend-rule.

signals.trigger: The moment any rule is taught or amended: classify it machine-enforceable or judgment and record the enforcement.
signals.why: teach/amend-rule is the teaching/amending act; the standing audit direction on violations is a separate non-action trigger.

signals.trigger: A squash merge (gh pr merge that merges, including --auto) is a commit boundary.
signals.why: Ledger boundary sweep at a commit or merge to main: a squash merge is one.

signals.trigger: A squash merge (gh pr merge that merges, including --auto) is a commit boundary.
signals.why: Committing: a squash merge is a commit boundary; whether the run's own paths were committed by name needs a reader.

signals.trigger: Commit your own written paths by name before a run ends, and again before any git checkout / checkout -b; change branch by taking a worktree.
signals.why: The rule fires 'before any git checkout/git checkout -b' unconditionally; its end-of-run trigger is not visible as a tool call.

signals.trigger: Committing: name each path, never `git add -A`/`-a`/`.`.
signals.why: A commit or bulk add is where the commit-by-named-path constraint binds.

signals.trigger: A squash merge (gh pr merge that merges, including --auto) is a commit boundary.
signals.why: A commit touching a gate script: a squash merge commits the PR's diff to main.

signals.trigger: When a commit touches a gate script or the enforcement map, re-bless the gate baseline in the same commit.
signals.why: A commit is necessary; whether it touches a gate or the enforcement map needs review.

signals.trigger: Same trigger through the ./run.sh call door.
signals.why: Bash door to the same paragraph-field write verbs.

signals.trigger: After any record write carrying long or multi-line text fields: re-read the row and assert no swallowed parameter tags or NULL fields.
signals.why: The rule binds after paragraph-field record writes (it lists these verbs 'and kin'); whether fields were long/multi-line needs review.

signals.trigger: Mail capture through the local mail stores.
signals.why: Local mail-store reads are the rule's mandated route.

signals.trigger: Mail capture on the partner's side reads local mail stores, never a Gmail API integration.
signals.why: Reading mail through the Gmail connector is the act the rule forbids for the partner's mail; whose mail was read needs review.

signals.trigger: Findings, enrichment results, record updates (and handoffs, checkpoints, status/audit writeups) go into the database, never a markdown report.
signals.why: The violating act is writing a markdown file; whether its content is a record or genuine doctrine/narrative needs review.

signals.trigger: When a vendor/client/lead/party is about to be created or updated with a wanted field blank: research it, do not ask the partner.
signals.why: Contact create/update is the stated moment; whether a wanted field was blank needs review.

signals.trigger: When any new contact enters the system (lead, client, vendor, party): run a deep open-source research pass before asking the partner anything.
signals.why: Creating a contact record is the entry event; contacts can also enter through a partner's words, and compliance needs review.

signals.trigger: When a subagent brief is written (or a running seat's scope is widened) for a sweep across disk, it carries a data-class boundary.
signals.why: The rule binds at brief-writing time; only briefs that send a seat across disk (file hunts, 'look everywhere') qualify, so each needs review.

signals.trigger: At creation of any scheduled task, trigger or subagent: done-condition, failure path, watched first run, run ledger.
signals.why: Creating a subagent or scheduled task is the rule's trigger; launchd/plist creation through Bash or Write can also bind without this signal.

signals.trigger: Driving CoStar: only the desktop app's Browser pane, never Chrome, one action at a time, no browser_batch, export via saved layouts.
signals.why: Any browser action on CoStar is the rule's trigger; compliance (which browser, batching) needs review.

signals.trigger: Deleting a published artifact.
signals.why: An artifact deletion is a deletion on a surface.

signals.trigger: Never delete (or tell the partner to delete) a file: move candidate deletions into a _to_delete staging folder.
signals.why: A file deletion command is the act the rule replaces with staging; whether the target is a candidate deletion (not throwaway temp) needs review.

signals.trigger: Before starting any task, name the executor; every subagent spawn picks the model that runs it, which is the rule's routing choice.
signals.why: A subagent spawn is a delegation whose model the rule governs (workforce, not the frontier model), so every Agent call binds; the second-mechanical-call tripwire can bind turns with no spawn.

signals.trigger: Delegation to an outside-model CLI seat is a routing choice the rule governs.
signals.why: Dispatching to an outside CLI seat is the rule's delegation lanes.
